name: ARTAS robotic system

lead: ARTAS is a robot from Restoration Robotics that finds and extracts donor hair follicles during FUE hair transplants. It was reported cleared by the FDA in 2011 for men.
It automates harvesting only; implantation still involves the surgical team. Registered trials compare it with manual harvest.

paras: Imaging maps the donor scalp and a dual-needle punch extracts follicular units.
Risks are those of FUE generally. Reference sources note higher cost and training requirements; no trial results were found in the sources reviewed.

lead: The ARTAS system is a computer-assisted robotic device for hair restoration, made by Restoration Robotics. It uses image guidance to identify and extract individual follicular units from the donor scalp in follicular unit extraction (FUE).[1][2]

Reference sources report US FDA clearance in 2011 for harvesting hair in men with androgenetic alopecia, and describe a system using high-definition imaging and a dual-needle punch.[1][2] Reported drawbacks include higher cost than manual FUE, limits to FUE-style harvesting and the need for trained operators.[2] ClinicalTrials.gov lists manufacturer-associated studies comparing computer-assisted and manual harvest, but no results were available in the sources reviewed.[3][4][5]

paras: According to a general reference, cameras map the donor area, and a dual-needle punch extracts follicular units; the cited punch depth is about 1 mm and the article cites transection rates under 5 percent and 400 to 800 grafts per hour.[2] Those numbers come from a reference page, not from trial data in the sources reviewed.

Wikipedia states the ARTAS system was approved by the FDA in 2011 for harvesting follicular units from men with brown or black hair.[1] Grokipedia describes the clearance as a 510(k) for men with androgenetic alopecia.[2]

Grokipedia lists costs 20 to 40 percent above manual FUE and the need for specialised training.[2] A Canadian aesthetic surgery meeting abstract argued that most hair restoration candidates are not appropriate for FUE whether manual, NeoGraft-assisted or ARTAS robotic.

No published results were found in the sources reviewed. Registered studies include a 2009 comparison of computer-assisted versus manual hair harvest (n=37),[3] a 2016 comparison of computer-assisted and manual implantation (n=32)[4] and a larger registered computer-assisted restoration study (n=150).[5]

timeline.event: FDA clearance of the ARTAS system for FUE harvesting.[1][2]
